
How does a change in treatment affect the average outcome? The first example
answers this question for a sample that includes zeros. The trade examples
then show how to hold fixed effects constant when making predictions, and
when a two-way model can estimate slopes without fitting those effects.

## 1. Fit ordinary power means

Suppose treatment is binary and the outcome is a count. To compare treated
and untreated observations at the same value of `control`, `ppml()` models
the arithmetic mean, including zeros. For comparison, `logols()` models
the geometric mean among observations with positive outcomes.

```{r ordinary}
library(powermean)
set.seed(20261120)

n <- 800L
data <- data.frame(treated = rbinom(n, 1, 0.4), control = rnorm(n))
data$outcome <- rpois(n, exp(0.5 + 0.35 * data$treated + 0.2 * data$control))

arithmetic <- ppml(outcome ~ treated + control, data)
geometric <- logols(outcome ~ treated + control, data, positive_only = TRUE)
tidy(arithmetic)
effect(arithmetic, "treated")
```

The fitted treatment coefficient is about 0.325. Its proportional effect,
`expm1(0.325)`, is about 0.384. At the same value of `control`, the fitted
arithmetic mean is **38.4% higher** for the treated group. PPML uses all
800 observations. The log regression uses the 671 with positive outcomes.

## 2. Prepare rows and reuse the design

`prepare()` lets you reuse the same formula and data. The next call changes
the target with `omega = 0.5`. It models the conditional mean of the square
root of the outcome, then squares that mean for prediction. The working
variance order `tau` controls how the estimating equation weights observations.
Use `$sample$positions` to find the original rows each fit used.

```{r prepared}
prepared <- prepare(outcome ~ treated + control, data)
half_order <- fit(prepared, omega = 0.5, tau = 1.5, vcov = "HC3")
c(n_arithmetic = arithmetic$sample$nobs, n_half_order = half_order$sample$nobs)
head(predict(half_order))
se(half_order)
```

## 3. Estimate a three-way gravity model

The panel has exporter-year, importer-year and directed pair fixed
effects. An agreement takes effect on different dates for different
pairs. In the formula, `exporter^year` gives each exporter its own effect in
each year. `importer^year` does the same for importers, and `pair` controls
for differences between trade partners that persist across years.

```{r gravity}
gravity <- expand.grid(exporter = seq_len(12L), importer = seq_len(12L),
                       year = seq_len(8L))
gravity <- gravity[gravity$exporter != gravity$importer, ]
gravity$pair <- interaction(gravity$exporter, gravity$importer, drop = TRUE)
adoption <- sample(2:12, nlevels(gravity$pair), replace = TRUE)
gravity$agreement <- as.integer(gravity$year >= adoption[as.integer(gravity$pair)])
gravity$trade <- rpois(nrow(gravity), exp(1.5 + 0.4 * gravity$agreement +
    sin(gravity$exporter * gravity$year) / 5 + cos(gravity$importer * gravity$year) / 5))

formula <- trade ~ 0 + agreement | pair + exporter^year + importer^year
joint <- ppml(formula, gravity, cluster = ~pair)
cancelled <- fit(formula, gravity, cancel = "pair", tau = 1)
etable(joint, cancelled, names = c("Joint PPML", "Pair-cancelled PPML"))
```

With `tau = 1`, cancelling the pair effects gives the same agreement
coefficient as joint PPML on the same observations. Cancelling at another
working variance changes the slope equation. See
`vignette("gravity", package = "powermean")` for the Gamma example
and the bias adjustments.

### Predict trade for the same pairs

What would predicted trade be if every pair had an agreement?
Change `agreement` on the rows the model used. Keep their row names, order,
and fixed-effect identifiers. Both predictions use the fitted slopes,
offsets and recovered fixed effects.

```{r gravity-prediction}
retained <- gravity[cancelled$sample$positions, , drop = FALSE]
with_agreement <- transform(retained, agreement = 1L)
head(fixef(cancelled)$pair)
head(cbind(observed = retained$trade, fitted = predict(cancelled),
           with_agreement = predict(cancelled, with_agreement),
           residual = residuals(cancelled)))
```

The first call returns a table with the pair labels and their estimated
log effects. You can also get all three fixed-effect tables with
`predict(cancelled, type = "fixed_effects")`. In the second call the residual
is observed trade minus fitted trade. Pairs that already have an agreement
keep their fitted trade in the counterfactual.

## 4. Difference out two fixed effects with GMM1 or GMM2

GMM1 and GMM2 compare four cells at a time. For instance, take two firms
observed in each of two years. Pair each firm's first observation with the
other firm's second observation. Each of the two resulting products contains
both firm effects and both year effects. Jochmans (2017) uses this symmetry
to remove the fixed effects from the slope equation.
[Two-Way Models for Gravity, §§I–III](https://doi.org/10.1162/REST_a_00620)

### What do the two-way moments assume?

Let $U_{ij}=Y_{ij}/\mu_{ij}$, where $\mu_{ij}$ is the exponential mean
including both fixed effects. Condition on the full regressor array and
all fixed effects, denoted by $\mathcal C$. The mean model gives
$E[U_{ij}\mid\mathcal C]=1$ in each cell. The two-way difference also uses
an assumption about the two diagonals of each rectangle,

$$
E[U_{ij}U_{k\ell}\mid\mathcal C]
  = E[U_{i\ell}U_{kj}\mid\mathcal C].
$$

This is an extra restriction. A shock shared by the two cells on just one
diagonal can change their expected product even when each cell still has
mean one. Under the conditions in Jochmans (2017), both expected products
equal one. The standard errors reported here assume conditionally independent
cell errors and that both dimensions grow.

The distinction matters when choosing weights. In a joint PML fit with
`omega = 1`, working variance $V(\mu)=\mu^\tau$ gives each relative residual
$Y/\mu-1$ weight $\mu^{2-\tau}$ in the slope equation. PPML weights it by
$\mu$ and Gamma PML gives it unit weight. These scores use the conditional
mean of one cell at a time. GMM1 and GMM2 weight the four-cell difference
differently, so their slopes can differ in a given sample. Both rely on
the same cross-product restriction.
[Benatia et al. (2026), §3.2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.11820v4)

### Fit a complete panel

The rectangular layout works for firms observed in every year. Supply one
row per firm and year, including observed zeros. Each dimension needs two
or more levels, and a single two-by-two rectangle gives too little
information for standard errors.

```{r gmm-rectangular}
panel <- expand.grid(firm = 1:5, year = 1:6)
cell <- seq_len(nrow(panel))
panel$log_price <- sin(cell)
panel$sales <- exp(-0.2 * panel$log_price + panel$firm / 8 -
    panel$year / 9) * (1 + 0.15 * cos(1.3 * cell))

sales_formula <- sales ~ 0 + log_price | firm + year
gmm1 <- fit(sales_formula, panel, estimator = "gmm1")
gmm2 <- fit(sales_formula, panel, estimator = "gmm2", start = coef(gmm1))
cbind(GMM1 = coef(gmm1), GMM2 = coef(gmm2))
confint(gmm2)
```

The estimated price elasticities are about −0.207 for GMM1 and −0.208 for
GMM2. Holding firm and year effects fixed, a 1% higher price corresponds
to about 0.21% lower expected sales. The second call uses the GMM1 slope as
a starting value. Each fit checks its own local solution.

### Fit directed pairs

For trade between countries in a single year, include every ordered pair
of distinct countries. This layout needs at least four countries and the
same country labels in the origin and destination columns.

```{r gmm-directed}
dyads <- expand.grid(origin = 1:6, destination = 1:6)
dyads <- dyads[dyads$origin != dyads$destination, ]
cell <- seq_len(nrow(dyads))
dyads$log_cost <- sin(cell)
dyads$trade <- exp(-0.2 * dyads$log_cost + dyads$origin / 8 -
    dyads$destination / 9) * (1 + 0.15 * cos(1.3 * cell))

directed <- fit(trade ~ 0 + log_cost | origin + destination, dyads,
                estimator = "gmm2", fe_layout = "directed")
stata <- with_vcov(directed, "stata")
cbind(paper = se(directed), stata = se(stata))
head(cbind(fitted = predict(directed), residual = residuals(directed)))
```

The default standard errors use the cell projections in Jochmans (2017).
To match Stata's `twgravity` convention, `with_vcov(directed, "stata")`
multiplies the covariance by `(n - 1) / n` for `n` countries. The slope
stays the same. For `predict(directed)`, Powermean holds that slope fixed
and recovers origin and destination effects by PPML. Fitted trade then
matches the observed totals by origin and by destination. Use
`fixef(directed)` for the two effect tables.

## 5. Compare standard errors

To see how a different covariance estimate affects the standard error of
the original treatment coefficient, use `with_vcov()`. It uses the same
observations and coefficients as `arithmetic`.

```{r retained}
alternative <- with_vcov(arithmetic, "HC3")
cbind(default = se(arithmetic), HC3 = se(alternative))
```
